One Number: 337 Stocks Rose and the Index Still Fell

On Thursday, October 22, 2026, 337 S&P 500 stocks finished higher. Only 159 declined and 1 was unchanged across 497 tracked constituents. The index still closed lower. What 337 Gainers Reveal About Your Index Fund

The S&P 500 is weighted by market value, so the biggest stocks have undue influence on the index's direction. Many investors use an index fund for broad market exposure, and those portfolios tilt heavily toward technology. One major S&P 500 index fund held 519 positions as of June 30, 2026, but Information Technology made up 38.0% of net assets and Communication Services added another 9.7%.

title: Billionaire Paul Tudor Jones warns AI and IPOs could hit stocks hard in 2027. Protect your nest egg now

Wall Street's appetite for artificial intelligence has helped fuel a stock market boom. But billionaire investor Paul Tudor Jones is worried about what happens when the bill comes due.

"2027 is going to be really, really challenging for the stock market," the Tudor Investment Corp. founder told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Oct. 13 (1).

Top Picks

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Goldco's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

His concern comes down to supply and demand. As companies raise money to fund the AI buildout and big names go public, more shares will compete for investors' dollars.

Jones expects that shift to make life harder for shareholders — and he plans to bet on falling prices.

"I'll be short the whole year," he said.

If you've benefited from rising stocks, it might be worth asking how much of your nest egg depends on the boom continuing.

More shares, more competition

For years, corporate buybacks and acquisitions have helped take shares off the market. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) alone repurchased 402 million shares for $89.3 billion in fiscal 2025 (2).

Acquisitions can also remove an entire company's stock from public trading. When Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) bought Activision Blizzard in 2023, it cancelled shareholders' stock in exchange for $95 per share in cash (3).

Jones tracks those forces against the stock coming onto the market through IPOs, additional offerings and the expiration of selling restrictions. He believes that balance is becoming less favorable for investors.

SpaceX's enormous valuation and the anticipated offerings from Anthropic and OpenAI are changing the calculation, he said. More companies seeking investor money could make it harder to sustain high stock prices.

An IPO also isn't necessarily the end of the selling. Employees, founders and early backers often face lockup periods that temporarily prevent them from unloading their shares.

Once those restrictions expire, more stock becomes available to trade. Those shareholders won't necessarily sell immediately, but buyers may eventually need to absorb substantial blocks of stock.

That creates a potential share overhang (4): The prospect of selling that could weigh on prices if demand doesn't keep pace.

The artificial intelligence (AI) investing thesis has been tough during the past month, but a bundle of tech earnings can change sentiment. Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), and Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) are some of the tech giants slated to report earnings by the end of the month, and these are the key details every investor should monitor.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

AI capital expenditures

If hyperscalers say that they will continue to ramp up spending, it gives chipmakers, neoclouds, and other companies at the center of the AI trade full permission to rebound.

Elon Musk offered some good news when SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX) reported earnings earlier this month. He told investors that hyperscalers and AI enterprises have been relentlessly "hound[ing]" SpaceX for more compute. Even SpaceX is struggling to find compute, with Musk expecting the superintelligence computing capacity shortage to last for years.

That backdrop suggests hyperscalers will spend more than expected and project even higher AI capital expenditures into the fourth quarter and beyond.

That would be good news, but it's equally important to assess how each company will fund its capital expenditures. Microsoft already told investors it would achieve positive free cash flow in its fiscal 2027, suggesting that the AI build-out is sustainable.

Revenue growth rates

All this spending has to translate into positive returns to justify the huge cost of the AI build-out. That's why investors should closely look at year-over-year growth rates for the tech giants. It's already clear that chipmakers are still doing well. Micron (NASDAQ: MU) posted 379% year-over-year revenue growth in its fiscal Q4 2026 as demand for its memory chips continues to soar.

However, all those chips have to translate into meaningful revenue growth rates for hyperscalers to justify the increased capital expenditures. Alphabet's cloud revenue, specifically, will be on my radar. That part of the business has been accelerating a lot lately, including an 82% year-over-year growth rate in the second quarter. The more Google Cloud's revenue growth rate accelerates in the third quarter, the better it is for the AI trade.

Profitability also matters, but there are two reasons I am not looking at net income as much. First, it's normal for tech innovations to be unprofitable for multiple years before enjoying dramatic profit margin expansion upon profitability. Google Cloud is a great example, since it was unprofitable for more than a decade.

title: Billionaire Ken Griffin Says We May Be in a Bubble. Here’s What History Says Happens Next.

Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks have driven stock market gains over the past several years amid excitement about this technology's potential. Some of these companies, such as chip designer Nvidia and cloud services provider Alphabet, have already started reaping the rewards. Demand for their AI products and services has supercharged revenue growth and their stock performance.

But the AI story isn't over, and to support ongoing growth, major investment is needed. And that's exactly why tech giants Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta Platforms aim to spend more than $700 billion on the infrastructure ramp-up this year. Those plans have sparked concern among investors, though, with the idea that the revenue opportunity may not justify such spending levels.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

In fact, some investors have even questioned whether a bubble may have formed. And one of those investors is Ken Griffin, founder and chief of Citadel. We're "almost certainly" in an AI bubble, the billionaire said in an interview with Bloomberg.

Let's take a closer look at Griffin's comments and check out what history says happens next.

Ken Griffin. Image source: Getty Images.

The early chapters of the AI story

First, though, let's page through the earlier chapters of the AI story. Over the past few years, companies have focused on training models, and this has created growth for all of the players involved, from chip designers and AI labs to the cloud service providers that offer customers access to these models.

Since many of these players are heavily weighted in the S&P 500, they helped lead the index to multiple record highs and a gain of nearly 100% since the start of 2023. Investors aimed to get in early on current and potential AI winners since the technology may be a game changer. It may streamline many processes, supercharge innovation, and, thanks to all of this and more, AI could significantly boost corporate earnings. Both the developers and users of AI may see earnings climb as this technology evolves and is used on a widespread basis.

Today, though, some investors worry that an AI bubble has formed, as stocks trade at record high levels. We can see, below, through the S&P 500 Shiller CAPE ratio, an inflation-adjusted view of stock prices relative to earnings, that stocks are trading near a peak.

Shiller CAPE Ratio data by YCharts

"There's almost certainly bubbles within this moment in time," Griffin told Bloomberg this week. "And any radical transformation of our economy is generally intertwined with a bubble."

Using history as a guide

This idea of economic transformation is key and allows us to use history as a guide. The last tech bubble was back in 2000, with the famous dot-com bubble. We can see the pattern in the chart below.

^SPX data by YCharts

Now, if we look at the index including those times all the way to today, we see that the dot-com bubble looks like a small event, and the S&P 500's performance over time clearly compensated -- and the index went on to soar well above even its highest dot-com bubble levels.

^SPX data by YCharts

Griffin's comments in the Bloomberg interview support this, as he says, referring to bubbles, that "the companies that are on the other side of that bubble are the market leaders for decades to come."

So, history is telling us two things about what happens next. If the market follows historical patterns, it may indeed decline in the coming weeks or months. But the good news is that it's always gone on to gain over the long run -- and so have quality stocks, even those involved in the particular bubble. For example, e-commerce giant Amazon, trading at about $5 per share during the dot-com bubble, crashed to less than $1 after the bubble burst. Today, the stock trades for more than $260.

What does this mean for investors? Even if a downturn or crash lies ahead, this is a temporary event, and the index and quality stocks will recover and gain. The best thing you can do is take a long-term view and hold on through market downturns -- your patience may be greatly rewarded over time.

title: UK on alert over Beijing-backed AI hacking spree
detail:
UK on alert over Beijing-backed AI hacking spree
National Cyber Security Centre · The Telegraph
Tom Saunders
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 1:30 AM EDT 4 min read
MSFT
Trade MSFT on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Britain's cyber security agency is urgently investigating a Beijing-backed hacking campaign amid fears that sensitive secrets were compromised.

The National Cyber Security Centre, an arm of GCHQ, is understood to be working with Microsoft and others to understand whether British organisations have been compromised by attacks from a group called "Storm-0940".

Microsoft last week uncovered a global campaign by the "China-state-aligned" hackers to target hundreds of organisations around the world using AI.

Sensitive industries, including defence, energy, finance, government and technology, were among those targeted, Microsoft said.

ConnectWise, an American company, was compromised as part of the attack. Its cloud service is used by major organisations to help back-up Microsoft 365 email and files.

ConnectWise has notified Britain's data watchdog about a breach, which the Information Commissioner's Office is assessing.

The supply-chain attack forced ConnectWise to suspend its services. The company said there was no sign that stored backups had been compromised, but warned that switching off its service would not remove any access the attackers had already gained to customers' systems.

Manny Rivelo, the chief executive of ConnectWise, said: "We contained the affected application connections and are restoring services in controlled phases.

"Those actions do not remove unauthorised access that may already have been established within individual customer tenants, which require separate review."

Microsoft said the China-linked hackers had been using AI to launch attacks since at least September and had successfully gained access to the cloud infrastructure of a number of organisations, sometimes in less than three hours.

"AI Agents are not constrained by factors affecting humans – they can work around the clock, on weekends, and on holidays and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously enabling significantly reduced time from selecting a target to achieving objectives, increasing the speed and impact of complex attacks," security researchers wrote.

It comes amid a barrage of AI-boosted hacking attempts over the past week. Websites around the world have been hit by millions of hacking attempts after AI agents discovered a vulnerability in PHP, a coding language.

The programming language underpins about 70pc of the world's websites, and the flaw led governments and companies to pull their websites off the internet before they could be attacked, and so they could patch the fault.
